source.title: Overparameterized multiple linear regression as hyper-curve fitting

record.file_problem: Whole paper text is present. The opening journal/date fields contain generic placeholders, but the main text is readable.
record.tranche_reason: The paper varies the training-set size/rank in synthetic overparameterized regression experiments and reports test prediction errors, a different setup from the double-descent sources.
record.gate_note: The paper mentions double descent in the introduction and cites prior work, but those citations are not results from this study. The relevant own results are Figure 2's test-error curves against training-set rank; other results on polynomial degree, noise, predictor removal, and the yarn dataset do not test the listed versions.
record.test_reason: Double descent appears only as a citation in the introduction. The only sample-size sweep (Fig. 2 top) uses noiseless data with n from 2 to 14 against p of 200 to 203 predictors. It never approaches the interpolation threshold n≈p and reports no test-error peak or rise, so it cannot bear on V3 or any other version. The aim is exact recovery once the training set reaches the dataset rank q.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is correct. The authors find overparameterized MLR equivalent to hyper-curve (IR) fitting on FOP datasets, with exact prediction once the training set is complete. They find that polynomial-degree truncation regularizes noisy data and that removing improper predictors improves prediction (yarn test error 0.28 to 0.05). They draw no conclusion about double descent.
record.recipe_differences: Synthetic overparameterized linear-regression experiments vary training-set rank and report relative test prediction errors; the paper does not reproduce the original double-descent procedure.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports different dataset ranks and predictor compositions; errors for high-degree or non-functional predictors do not reach machine precision.

fits_no_version.finding: In noiseless fundamentally overparameterized linear data (p≫n), minimum-norm MLR/IR test error drops to near machine precision once the training set rank reaches the dataset rank q. The drop is less complete with high-degree or non-functional predictors.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In rank-deficient overparameterized linear regression, test error collapses when training samples reach the data's intrinsic rank q, well below the predictor count p.

fits_no_version.finding: Authors note training-validation y-error far below test error at the optimal degree r*. They call this benign overfitting and attribute it to the monomial basis choice.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Benign overfitting in the polynomial IR model arises from the basis choice rather than from noise statistics.

record.problems: The relevant numerical test-error values are shown only in a figure, with no uncertainty estimates. The experiments are synthetic and limited to the stated predictor constructions.
record.rows_left_out: No other rows bear on the listed versions: Figure 2's polynomial-degree sweep is not a model-capacity or epoch sweep, and the later noise, regularization, predictor-removal, and yarn-data results do not report a listed double-descent behavior.

untested.parts: No deep networks and no model-size sweep.
Sample sweep stays far below n=p and uses noiseless data, so no test near the interpolation threshold.
No capacity sweep through an interpolation point.
No effective-complexity predictor of peak location.
Noise and polynomial-truncation regularization are studied, but not in relation to any double-descent peak.
No effective-parameter re-plotting of a double-descent curve.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V3 limits_scope label is dropped. The setting never crosses the interpolation threshold and is noiseless, so the absence of a rise says nothing about the version.

versions.untested_parts: The experiments use synthetic noiseless datasets and do not establish a general effect near an interpolation threshold across other settings.
No capacity sweep across model classes or test of a general post-interpolation risk curve.
No single effective-complexity measure is evaluated as a predictor of peak location.
Noise and regularization are studied, but the paper does not test whether they drive, split, or eliminate a double-descent peak.
No comparison of double descent with a curve measured against effective parameter count.

rows.note: The text says prediction errors drop once the training dataset becomes complete; it does not describe a test-error increase as sample count rises.
rows.check: Sweep covers n≤14 with p=200 and noiseless data, far below the n=p interpolation threshold V3 names. The values are figure-only and no rise or peak is described. The row measures exact recovery at dataset completeness (n=q), not more-data harm.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: The three synthetic noiseless datasets in Figure 2
reader_labels.reason: The reported test errors drop as training rank reaches dataset completeness rather than rising with more samples in these settings (R1–R3). This qualifies where the claimed more-data harm is observed; it does not rule out such harm in other settings.
